title: Streamlined Flow in Hydrodynamics
short_intro: Streamlined flow (or laminar flow) is a regime of fluid motion in which each particle of the fluid follows a smooth path, called a streamline, such that the paths of different particles never cross each other. At any given point in the fluid, the velocity vector of the fluid particles remains constant with respect to time.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of streamline, laminar vs turbulent flow, equation of continuity for incompressible fluids, and basic applications of Bernoulli's theorem.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Velocity potential and stream function in two-dimensional flows, Euler's equation of motion along a streamline, and irrotational conditions linked to angular momentum and central forces.

prerequisites: Centre of mass and translational kinematics
Angular momentum conservation in central forces
Pressure, density, and basic Newtonian mechanics

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Characteristics of Streamlines
bullets: A streamline is an imaginary curve drawn in a fluid such that the tangent at any point on it gives the direction of the velocity vector of the fluid particle at that point.
Two streamlines can never intersect, as an intersection would imply two different velocity vectors at a single point, violating the steady-state assumption.
In steady flow, streamlines coincide identically with particle pathlines and streaklines.

concept_notes.heading: Equation of Continuity
bullets: Based on the principle of conservation of mass applied to an incompressible fluid flowing through a tube of varying cross-sectional area.
The product of the cross-sectional area (A) and the fluid velocity (v) remains constant along any flow tube: Av = constant.
Physical interpretation: Where the pipe constricts, the velocity of the fluid increases; where the pipe widens, the velocity decreases.

concept_notes.heading: Condition for Streamlined to Turbulent Transition
bullets: Determined by the dimensionless Reynolds number (R<sub>e</sub> = ρvd/η).
For flow in a cylindrical pipe, streamlined flow is strictly maintained when R<sub>e</sub> is less than the critical value (typically ~2000).
Higher velocities, larger tube diameters, or lower fluid viscosities destabilize streamlines, transitioning the flow into chaotic turbulence.

concept_notes.heading: Irrotational vs Rotational Flow
bullets: In an ideal streamlined flow, if fluid elements possess no net angular velocity about their center of mass (ω = 0), the flow is termed irrotational.
Irrotational flow permits the definition of a scalar velocity potential function (φ), simplifying mathematical analysis.
Viscous boundary layers introduce local rotation (vorticity), modifying pure potential streamlined flow near solid boundaries.

derivations.title: Equation of Continuity Derivation
derivations.conditions: Steady, one-dimensional flow of an incompressible fluid through a rigid pipe
steps: Consider a non-uniform pipe segment with cross-sectional areas A<sub>1</sub> and A<sub>2</sub> at entry and exit.
Let the fluid densities be ρ<sub>1</sub> and ρ<sub>2</sub>, and velocities be v<sub>1</sub> and v<sub>2</sub> respectively.
In a small time interval Δt, the mass entering the left cross-section is m<sub>1</sub> = A<sub>1</sub> v<sub>1</sub> ρ<sub>1</sub> Δt.
Similarly, the mass leaving the right cross-section is m<sub>2</sub> = A<sub>2</sub> v<sub>2</sub> ρ<sub>2</sub> Δt.
By conservation of mass for a steady flow, m<sub>1</sub> = m<sub>2</sub>, giving A<sub>1</sub> v<sub>1</sub> ρ<sub>1</sub> = A<sub>2</sub> v<sub>2</sub> ρ<sub>2</sub>.
For an incompressible fluid (ρ<sub>1</sub> = ρ<sub>2</sub> = ρ), this simplifies to A<sub>1</sub> v<sub>1</sub> = A<sub>2</sub> v<sub>2].

derivations.title: Euler's Equation of Motion Along a Streamline
derivations.conditions: Inviscid, steady flow along a streamline under conservative body forces
steps: Consider a fluid element of mass dm = A ds ρ along a streamline, where ds is the length element.
Forces acting on the element in the direction of flow are pressure forces and component of gravity: (P)A - (P + \frac{\partial P}{\partial s} ds)A - \rho A ds g \cos\theta = dm \cdot a.
Substitute dm = ρ A ds and acceleration a = v \frac{\dv}{ds}.
Simplify and divide throughout by ρ A ds, utilizing \cos\theta = \frac{dz}{ds} where z is vertical height.
Rearrange terms to group pressure, kinetic energy, and potential energy gradients together.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Velocity Profile in Laminar Pipe Flow
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A parabolic velocity distribution curve across the diameter of a circular pipe, showing maximum velocity at the center and zero velocity at the inner walls (no-slip condition).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Viscous drag retards fluid layers near the wall, whereas the central core experiences minimal shear constraint, forming a parabolic profile.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested conceptually in TGT/PGT matching questions regarding parabolic distribution vs plug flow.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Reynolds Dye Experiment Setup
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A glass tank containing water with a central fine nozzle injecting colored dye into a horizontal glass tube where flow rate can be controlled via a valve.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: At low velocities, the dye forms a distinct, straight, unblended filament (streamlined). As velocity increases past critical, the filament wavers and disperses completely (turbulent).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Direct theoretical foundation questions regarding the experimental criteria of critical velocity and Reynolds number.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Streamlines Around an Obstacle (Airfoil/Sphere)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Smooth, continuous flow lines diverging and converging symmetrically around a streamlined body without detachment points.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates irrotational flow conservation where flow lines crowd over the upper curved surface of an airfoil, indicating localized velocity increase.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used in PGT questions analyzing pressure differentials and lift generation.

solved_numericals.question: Water flows through a horizontal pipe whose internal diameter changes from 4 cm to 2 cm. If the speed of water at the wider section is 2 m s<sup>-1</sup>, find its speed at the narrower section.
solution_steps: Identify given values: d<sub>1</sub> = 4 cm, v<sub>1</sub> = 2 m s<sup>-1</sup>, d<sub>2</sub> = 2 cm.
Area is proportional to diameter squared: A ∝ d<sup>2</sup>.
Apply the equation of continuity: A<sub>1</sub> v<sub>1</sub> = A<sub>2</sub> v<sub>2</sub> ⇒ d<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup> v<sub>1</sub> = d<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup> v<sub>2</sub>.
Solve for v<sub>2</sub>: 16 × 2 = 4 × v<sub>2</sub> ⇒ v<sub>2</sub> = 32 / 4 = 8 m s<sup>-1</sup>.

solved_numericals.question: A two-dimensional incompressible flow field is given by the velocity components u = 2xy and v = x<sup>2</sup> - y<sup>2</sup>. Determine whether the flow is possible (satisfies continuity) and if it is irrotational.
solution_steps: Check continuity condition for 2D incompressible flow: ∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y = 0.
Sum them: 2y + (-2y) = 0. Therefore, the continuity equation is satisfied and the flow is physically possible.
Substitute: ω<sub>z</sub> = 1/2 (2x - 2x) = 0. Thus, the flow is irrotational.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the maximum velocity for steady streamlined flow of water (viscosity η = 10<sup>-3</sup> Pa s, density ρ = 1000 kg m<sup>-3</sup>) through a pipe of diameter 5 cm, assuming the critical Reynolds number is 2000.
solution_steps: Write down the Reynolds number formula: R_e = ρ v d / η.
Rearrange to solve for velocity v: v = (R_e × η) / (ρ × d).
Substitute given values: R<sub>e</sub> = 2000, η = 10<sup>-3</sup> Pa s, ρ = 1000 kg m<sup>-3</sup>, d = 0.05 m.

assumptions_and_limitations: The fluid is assumed to be completely incompressible (ρ = constant), which is valid for liquids but breaks down for high-speed gases where compressibility effects dominate.

Internal friction or fluid viscosity is neglected in ideal streamlined flow derivations like Bernoulli's theorem, requiring correction via Navier-Stokes equations for real viscous fluids near boundaries.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Streamlines represent the physical trajectory of a single moving fluid particle under all conditions.
common_misconceptions.correct: Streamlines represent instantaneous velocity field tangents; they match particle pathlines only when the flow is strictly steady.
common_misconceptions.why: In unsteady flow fields, the velocity vector at a spatial point changes with time, causing pathlines and streamlines to diverge.

common_misconceptions.wrong: An increase in fluid velocity inside a constricted pipe implies an increase in pressure due to crowding.
common_misconceptions.correct: An increase in velocity results in a decrease in static pressure, as dictated by Bernoulli's energy conservation principle.
common_misconceptions.why: Kinetic energy per unit volume increases at constrictions, requiring a corresponding drop in static pressure energy term.

quick_revision: Streamlines never intersect and their tangent gives the instantaneous flow direction.
The continuity equation (A<sub>1</sub>v<sub>1</sub> = A<sub>2</sub>v<sub>2</sub>) stems directly from conservation of mass for incompressible fluids.
Critical Reynolds number (~2000 in pipes) marks the boundary between laminar (streamlined) and turbulent flow regimes.
